Article Title: Who is Seema Kaliramna? The mother and PhD scholar who won Commonwealth Games 2026 bronze
Article Text:
Seema Kaliramna (Image credit: X)

Who is Seema Kaliramna ?



Dedicated CWG medal to her husband

NEW DELHI: Indian discus thrower Seema Kaliramna won bronze medal in the women's discus throw at the Commonwealth Games 2026 in Glasgow. She secured third place with a best throw of 58.65m.Seema had only two valid throws in six attempts. After starting with a foul, Seema reached 57.32m and then threw to 58.65 before ending her campaign with three foul throws. But the 58.65m was enough to earn her a bronze medal.Jamaica's Samantha Hall claimed the gold medal with a Games-leading throw of 61.66m, while Canada's Julia Tunks won silver with 60.67m.Seema is one of India's top discus throwers from Haryana. Along with being an athlete, she is also pursuing a PhD in Physical Education at Chaudhary Bansi Lal University (CBLU) in Bhiwani.Her father, a former basketball player and javelin thrower in the Indian Army, introduced her to sports at a young age.Today, she is coached by her husband, Ravinder Kaliramna, popularly known as Monu Kaliramna, who is a former national-level discus thrower.After the birth of her son, Rudra, Seema took a break from athletics.However, she made an inspiring comeback just 11 months later, balancing training, motherhood and her PhD studies.She won the gold medal at the 2025 National Games and later claimed the national title. At the National Inter-State Senior Athletics Championships in Bhubaneswar, she produced a personal best throw of 59.73m to qualify for the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.Seema has represented India at several international events, including the Youth Asian Championships. She also won gold at the first Khelo India University Games in 2020.Seema credited her husband and coach Ravinder for her CWG success."I am very happy. This was my first Commonwealth Games, and winning a bronze medal makes it even more special. I did not face any major difficulties during the competition. The only challenge was the cold weather, because I had to keep warming up repeatedly. Overall, it was a very good competition," Seema said."My husband arrived just two days ago. He [her son] was telling me to take him along, but this is a very emotional moment. My situation is such that I cannot bring my son with me. It is extremely difficult and painful. You can call it a sacrifice," she said."AFI has supported me tremendously, and SAI has also played a big role in my journey. Whenever I needed anything else, my family was always there to support me. I would like to dedicate this medal to my husband. All the hard work and sacrifices behind this achievement have been possible because of his constant support," Seema said.
Article Summary: Seema Kaliramna won bronze medal in the women's discus throw at the Commonwealth Games 2026 in Glasgow. She secured third place with a best throw of 58.65m. Seema credited her husband and coach Ravinder for her CWG success.

Article Title: Why Bankipur bypoll grabbed national attention and what it means for Prashant Kishor
Article Text:
PK is making a second attempt to establish himself as an electoral force by staking his claim in the Bankipur bypoll

Why Bankipur is being watched closely

Tough road for BJP?

Why it’s an all-at-stake contest for PK

Challenge for RJD

What the opinion poll says

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Will Bihar's Bankipur stand with the BJP , as it has over the years, or will it give Prashant Kishor a victory on debut? Or, will Tejashwi Yadav's RJD will finally have something to cheer about? The fate of the three key contenders in the crucial byelection have been sealed in EVM machines and the people's verdict will be known on August 3, when the votes are counted. So, what made this by-election grab so much of national attention?The Bankipur bypoll was necessitated after Nitin Nabin , who represented the urban Patna seat for nearly two decades, resigned from Bihar assembly to become a member of Rajya Sabha. This followed his elevation as BJP president earlier this year. The Bankipur seat has been a BJP bastion for over three decades with Nitin Nabin's family winning from the constituency for over 35 years. Before Nitin Nabin, the constituency was represented by his father Nabin Kishore Prasad Sinha. And that explains why winning today's election is so important for the BJP.But what could have been a cakewalk for BJP and its chief Nitin Nabin was turned into a formidable challenge with the entry of election strategist turned politician Prashant Kishor in the election arena. Kishor's entry made today's election a three-cornered contest.For Prashant Kishor, whose party Jan Suraj was outrightly rejected by the people of the state in the assembly elections last year, this bypoll is a litmus test. Kishor, who has scripted success stories of several parties and leaders as an election-strategist, would hope that the people of Bankipur would give his political career a much-needed boost.And finally the RJD, the third pole of this electoral battle, would desperately hope that the people of Bankipur would have voted today for a change. The RJD, which was literally decimated by the ruling NDA in the 2025 assembly elections, will be keen to prove a political point.Polling concluded with a voter turnout of 34.16 per cent among the nearly 3.8 lakh eligible electors, with counting of votes scheduled for August 3.As expected, the polling today was marked by allegations and counter allegations. Both Prashant Kishor and RJD candidate Rekha Gupta trained their guns at the BJP. Prashant Kishore alleged that more than 30 of his party workers had been arrested during polling and accused the police administration of acting "completely one-sidedly" to intimidate voters and help the BJP. "In an organised manner, wherever people of Jan Suraaj have set up tables, these people are taking them away. Across entire Bankipur, it's evident that it's not the BJP contesting this bypoll but the police force. People are being intimidated right from the night by going to their homes; some are being arrested," he said.RJD candidate Rekha Gupta accused BJP workers of violating the Model Code of Conduct by allegedly attempting to influence voters at polling stations. “The BJP has hatched a conspiracy. All the polling agents have been given BJP ID cards,” Gupta alleged, while urging the election authorities to take note of the matter," she said.The BJP rubbished these charges and instead accused that Jan Suraaj Party workers were "attempting to cast fraudulent votes" in the Bankipur assembly bypoll and urged the Election Commission to strengthen verification of electors. BJP state general secretary Nitin Abhishek wrote a letter to the returning officer of the assembly, claiming that such practices undermine the fundamental principles of democracy."It has come to our notice that representatives and workers associated with the Jan Suraaj Party are attempting to compromise the integrity of the polling process by attempting to cast fraudulent/fake votes in the Bankipur bypoll," the BJP said in the letter.Bypolls, anywhere in the country, attract little interest. For the NDA, which won 202 out of 243 seats in the assembly elections, the result of one seat should hardly matter.However, this bypoll is the first election after Samrat Choudhary took over the chief ministerial post from Nitish Kumar.The assembly election was fought with the NDA projecting Nitish as its chief ministerial face. However, Nitish resigned from the top post to take up a Rajya Sabha seat, handing over the reins to Choudhary.The Bankipur bypoll offers the first electoral test of public approval for Choudhary as chief minister.Realising the importance of the seat, the BJP left little to chance in Bankipur. The party mobilised an entire roster of NDA ministers, former ministers, MPs and MLAs to campaign for its candidate, Neeraj Kumar Sinha.Former chief minister Nitish Kumar also joined the campaign through a video appeal, urging voters to support the BJP candidate. On the ground, the party kept up a hectic schedule of bike rallies, Adhivakta Samwad, Chikitsa Samwad, roadshows and door-to-door outreach in an effort to consolidate support.Bankipur’s caste composition also makes the bypoll an interesting contest. The constituency has nearly 3.8 lakh voters, with Kayasths and Yadavs together making up around 25 per cent of the electorate.The BJP has traditionally enjoyed strong support among Kayasths. Muslims and Chandravanshis together account for nearly 20 per cent of voters, while Vaishyas, Dalits, Bhumihars, Rajputs, Brahmins, Kurmis and Kushwahas each constitute between 3 per cent and 8 per cent of the electorate.Prashant Kishor’s political gambit, along with developments such as Bharat Tiwari’s encounter and the recent student protests in Patna, has made the bypoll harder for the BJP than the party initially anticipated.The first setback came even before the campaign gathered pace. The BJP’s initial candidate, Abhishek Kumar Sinha, withdrew from the contest after reports emerged that a close family member had been convicted in the fodder scam.The BJP later replaced him with 32-year-old Neeraj Kumar Sinha after the party’s Central Election Committee approved his candidature.Another challenge for the ruling party is the reported resentment among sections of the upper-caste community following the June encounter of Bharat Tiwari.Tiwari was killed during a standoff with the police and Special Task Force personnel on June 17. In the aftermath, chief minister Samrat Choudhary met Tiwari’s family and assured them of a transparent investigation, the preservation of evidence and strict action against those found guilty.The recent student unrest has added another dimension to the campaign. Bankipur is home to several colleges, universities and coaching institutes, making students a significant voting bloc in the constituency.Large student protests over issues such as employment, education and alleged irregularities in competitive examinations have heightened political engagement among young voters.Police action during some of these demonstrations also attracted widespread attention on social media, ensuring that education, jobs and governance remain central themes in the bypoll campaign.Both Kishor and RJD working president Tejashwi Yadav blamed Samrat Choudhary for the action against protesters.The state government, too, was quick to respond. After a Bihar bandh called by Left-wing student unions on July 25, police detained close to 700 protesters, of whom nearly half were let off after they turned out to be minors.While talking to The Times of India, political analyst Kumar Vijay predicted a tough contest on July 30."BJP initially thought this election would be fairly easy. Perhaps that’s why it made a mistake in choosing its candidate. And when the second candidate was chosen, he too appeared to be a potentially weak opponent to Prashant Kishor, despite the constituency having several prominent leaders to choose from," Vijay said."But now BJP is seeing this contest turn tight. That’s why it has fielded 50 star campaigners for a single bypoll. And wherever these leaders have gone to campaign, they have faced opposition. This did not happen earlier," he told TOI.He added that if Prashant Kishor manages to consolidate Muslim, Yadav, women and fringe voters, it could spell trouble for the BJP."It is time for the BJP to reconsider its strategy, way of working and decision-making process," he added.Meanwhile, BJP state vice-president Santosh Pathak asserted that the party would easily win the bypoll. Although he acknowledged resentment among upper-caste voters, he claimed that they would ultimately vote for the BJP on July 30."Prashant Kishor’s entry has only added glamour to the election. Beyond that, there is nothing new about this contest. This time too, we will win by a good margin," Pathak said while talking to The Times of India."There is some resentment among Brahmins and Bhumihars, but they will still vote for the BJP. Bankipur is a backward-oriented seat. The people creating all the buzz are not voters of this assembly constituency," he added.Describing the contest as a “referendum” on the two-month-old BJP-led NDA government in Bihar, Prashant sought to transform what would ordinarily have been a local bypoll into one of the state’s most closely watched electoral battles."The upcoming by-election is going to be a referendum on the working of the two-month-old government of Samrat Choudhary," Prashant had said after announcing his candidature."If the BJP wins, I will have no hesitation in conceding that the saffron party continues to enjoy public support. If we win, it shall be for them to read the writing on the wall," he added.Despite several prominent leaders leaving Jan Suraaj, Kishor remained visible through mohalla meetings, adda baithaks, chai baithaks, padyatras, interactions with intellectuals and Jan Samwad programmes.However, the bypoll is also a test of Kishor’s own political project.A victory would give Jan Suraaj its first electoral breakthrough and help the party carve out political space in Bihar.A defeat, however, would make the road to revival even harder for the party. With no major election scheduled in Bihar before the 2029 Lok Sabha polls, the stakes could hardly be higher.This bypoll carries almost as much weight for the RJD, which put in a lacklustre show in the assembly elections and is now keen to keep its Muslim-Yadav vote bank from eroding. At the same time, Prashant Kishor’s rising profile, even if symbolic for now and confined to a single seat, poses a different kind of threat: the RJD cannot afford to cede its place as the principal challenger to the BJP.That dilemma captures the existential challenge confronting Tejashwi Yadav’s party. Should Jan Suraaj emerge as the leading anti-BJP force in Bankipur, it would inevitably chip away at the RJD’s standing as Bihar’s primary opposition party.The RJD has fielded Rekha Gupta, also known as Rekha Kumari , for the bypoll. She had contested the same seat in the November 2025 assembly polls, where she secured close to 47,000 votes.An opinion poll by VoteVibe suggests that the BJP retains the upper hand in Bankipur, but Prashant Kishor’s entry has transformed what was once seen as a one-sided contest.The survey projects the BJP to secure 44.9 per cent of the vote, comfortably ahead of Jan Suraaj at 33.8 per cent, while the RJD is estimated to finish a distant third with 17.8 per cent.The RJD appears to have suffered the biggest setback. According to the poll, its vote share is projected to decline from 29.8 per cent in the 2025 assembly polls to 17.8 per cent in Bankipur.The Bankipur bypoll has all the makings of a David and Goliath contest, though it is not entirely clear who fits which role. The BJP appears to be the giant. It has held the seat continuously since 1995, is backed by the resources of the ruling government and has deployed 50 star campaigners for a single bypoll.Yet the party enters the contest on the defensive after replacing its initial candidate and grappling with discontent among sections of its traditional upper-caste support base.PK, by contrast, looks like David, a challenger with no seats to his name and a party still finding its feet after last year's washout. But he carries the slingshot of celebrity, momentum from Bihar’s student protests and a campaign built entirely around unseating the giant.
Article Summary: Bankipur seat has been a BJP bastion for over three decades with Nitin Nabin's family winning from the constituency for over 35 years. Prashant Kishor's entry made today's election a three-cornered contest. The RJD, which was literally decimated by the ruling NDA in the 2025 assembly elections, will be keen to prove a political point.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Bhagat Singh: ‘Study so that you are able to meet the arguments of your opponents,’ and why knowledge is the strongest answer to disagreement
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Bhagat Singh

“Study so that you are able to meet the arguments of your opponents.” —

Bhagat Singh

Reading broadens the argument before it strengthens it

Knowledge changes the quality of disagreement

Why the quote still matters

Every disagreement presents a choice. One person raises their voice, while another repeats familiar slogans. A third begins asking questions, searching for evidence and trying to understand where the other side is coming from before responding. Bhagat Singh's advice belongs firmly in the third tradition. He treats study as preparation for conversation rather than examination, and knowledge as something that sharpens judgement instead of feeding pride. His words suggest that the strength of an argument depends less on confidence than on how carefully it has been built.Bhagat Singh wrote constantly throughout his short life. While imprisoned, he read history, economics, political philosophy, literature and revolutionary thought with remarkable discipline, filling notebooks with quotations and reflections from writers across the world. His reading shaped his politics, though it also shaped the way he argued. He believed conviction carried greater weight when it rested on careful thought instead of emotion alone. That is why this line continues to resonate. It speaks to anyone who hopes to persuade rather than simply win.People usually begin with opinions. Study asks them to examine where those opinions come from. A reader who spends time with different authors soon discovers that intelligent people have disagreed about almost every important question in history.Freedom, justice, religion, economics and education have all been debated across generations, often by thinkers who arrived at very different conclusions while drawing on equally serious scholarship.That process does something valuable. It slows certainty. Someone who has read widely becomes more careful with conclusions because they understand how many perspectives exist beyond their own experience. A lawyer prepares by studying both sides of a case. A scientist examines competing explanations before accepting one. A historian compares sources instead of relying on a single account. Strong arguments grow from that habit of testing ideas before defending them.Bhagat Singh encouraged the same discipline. He wanted young people to read because reading develops the habit of thinking independently. A belief borrowed from someone else can be repeated. A belief reached through study can be explained, defended and refined.Modern life makes it easy to respond immediately. Social media rewards quick reactions, television debates often value interruption over discussion and public conversations frequently become contests of personality rather than ideas. In that environment, Bhagat Singh's advice feels remarkably current.Knowledge does not eliminate disagreement. It changes the way disagreement is handled. A person who understands the history behind an issue is less likely to reduce it to slogans. Someone familiar with evidence can separate facts from assumptions. Even when no agreement is reached, the conversation becomes more useful because each side has something substantial to contribute.Many of history's greatest debates produced progress because participants challenged one another with ideas rather than insults. Scientific discoveries emerged through criticism. Constitutional democracies developed through public debate. Universities exist because questioning accepted wisdom has always been considered an essential part of learning. Those traditions survive only when people value understanding as much as persuasion.Education is often treated as a path towards employment, and it certainly serves that purpose. Bhagat Singh points to another purpose that receives far less attention. Reading equips people to think clearly when confronted with difficult questions. It teaches them to recognise weak reasoning, appreciate strong evidence and remain open to learning even while defending deeply held beliefs.That lesson extends far beyond politics. Families resolve differences through conversation. Workplaces depend on people exchanging ideas without resentment. Democracies function because citizens weigh competing arguments before making choices. In each of those settings, knowledge becomes more than personal achievement.It becomes a public responsibility.Bhagat Singh's words endure because they place faith in the power of ideas. They remind readers that disagreement has never been settled by volume alone. Lasting influence belongs to those who understand an issue well enough to answer it with reason, evidence and the patience to keep learning.
Article Summary: Bhagat Singh wrote constantly throughout his short life. While imprisoned, he read history, economics, political philosophy, literature and revolutionary thought. His reading shaped his politics, though it also shaped the way he argued. He believed conviction carried greater weight when it rested on careful thought.

Article Title: 'May do same with Army': Opposition attacks BJP for India Hockey's saffron jersey
Article Text:
Oppn attacks BJP over hockey jersey colour change to saffron

Why was the jersey changed?

NEW DELHI: Opposition on Thursday targeted Centre over the change in the hockey teams' jersey colour from the traditional blue to saffron and expressed concerns that the army's uniform could be next target.The group also accused the BJP and the RSS of trying to impose saffron across institutions.The remarks came after Hockey India unveiled new saffron jerseys for the national men's and women's teams ahead of next month's FIH Hockey World Cup in the Netherlands and Belgium. Hockey India has said the change was made following feedback from players and coaches, who felt the blue jersey blended with the blue synthetic turf, affecting on-field visibility.Reacting to the development, Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra alleged that the BJP and RSS were attempting to reshape institutions and history."Whether they change uniforms or try to rewrite history through education policy, no matter what they do... You have seen what the youth of our country think about this. You heard what the young people gathered at Jantar Mantar were saying. This is the voice of the nation.The struggle for this country's independence was founded on non-violence and truth; the RSS played no part in it," she said."The entire nation knows the reality, and those who didn't are now realising what their true intentions are. The Congress party led that movement under the guidance of Mahatma Gandhi, and the very soul of this country is rooted in non-violence, truth, and brotherhood. No one can take that away—not the RSS, nor anyone else. No matter how much they sow division, incite violence, or spread hatred, the country's soul—defined by brotherhood, mutual love, and unity—remains intact; they cannot strip that away," she added.Congress MP Amar Singh accused the BJP of attempting to 'saffronise' everything."Today they have done this with hockey; tomorrow they may do the same with the Army. How can anyone trust them? They want saffron everywhere," he said.Calling the move 'very unfortunate', Singh said no political party should change symbols that carry historical significance."Everything has its own history and significance. But they simply do not stop. What can we do?" he added.Congress leader Tariq Anwar also criticised the decision, saying it reflected the BJP's 'narrow-minded ideology'."Whether it is in the field of education or other sectors, there is an attempt to impose a particular ideology everywhere. This controversy is a symbol of that narrow-minded thinking," he said.Trinamool Congress leader Kirti Azad, however, said a team's performance mattered more than the colour of its jersey."As for the orange colour versus green, that doesn't really matter. Performance should matter on the field. Even in cricket, we used to play in white clothes. It does not come from colours; it comes from performance," he said."You achieve it through your own effort. So, it is not about the colour of the clothes; it is about your ability in the sport," Azad added.At the same time, he questioned the need to replace the traditional blue jersey."If blue has traditionally been the colour associated with our sports, then it should remain so. Why impose a religious colour on it?" he said.Hockey India has defended the move, saying the decision was based on technical feedback from players and coaches, who found that the blue jersey merged with the blue synthetic playing surface used in international hockey, affecting visibility during matches.The federation said saffron was chosen after considering several alternative colours, adding that it also symbolises courage, sacrifice and national pride as one of the colours of the Indian national flag.The new jersey will be worn by both the men's and women's teams during the FIH Hockey World Cup, scheduled to be held in the Netherlands and Belgium from August 15 to 30.Former India captain Viren Rasquinha had criticised the move, saying the blue jersey represented the team's legacy and identity, while Hockey India maintained that changes in jersey colours were not unprecedented, observing that the national team had previously worn yellow in the 2014 World Cup and sky blue in the 2018 edition.
Article Summary: Opposition accuses BJP and RSS of trying to impose saffron across institutions. Hockey India has said the change was made following feedback from players and coaches. The new jersey will be worn by both the men's and women's teams during the FIH Hockey World Cup.

Article Title: '20 traitors of Bengal': TMC's Kalyan Banerjee wears poster with rebel MPs' photos in Parl, seeks swift ECI decision

NEW DELHI: Trinamool Congress (TMC) suspended MP Kalyan Banerjee on Thursday staged a protest in Parliament against the defection of party MPs, wearing a poster displaying photographs of 20 rebel legislators and calling them "traitors of West Bengal. ""20 traitors of West Bengal are present in Parliament... dishonest people," Banerjee was heard saying while staging a protest.The protest comes after at least 20 of the TMC's 28 Lok Sabha MPs broke away from the party and joined the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI), pledging support to the NDA.The Trinamool Congress has described the rebel MPs as "gaddar" (traitors).The list of rebel MPs includes Sudip Bandyopadhyay, Rachna Banerjee, Jagadish Chandra Barma, Partha Bhowmick, Arup Chakraborty, Deepak Adhikari, Sayani Ghosh, Bapi Haldar, Abu Taher Khan, Kalipada Saren Kherwal, Asit Kumar and Kakoli Ghosh Dastidar, among others.Speaking to ANI earlier, Banerjee said the rebel MPs had approached the Election Commission regarding the split but no decision had been communicated so far.Calling for an early decision, Banerjee said prolonged uncertainty had political consequences. "Justice must be rooted in confidence; confidence should not be compromised. The matter has been left pending for so long. Granting them more time causes inconvenience.There is also a political ramification to this," he said.Earlier in the day, Banerjee also had a brief exchange with Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra outside Makar Dwar over the political history between the Congress and the TMC. Priyanka Gandhi remarked, "You took them from Congress to TMC," to which Banerjee responded, " Mamata Banerjee was thrown out of Congress in 1997."Priyanka Gandhi then said, "Rajiv Gandhi always promoted Mamata Banerjee," a remark to which Banerjee agreed.
Article Summary: The protest comes after at least 20 of the TMC's 28 Lok Sabha MPs broke away from the party and joined the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI) The Trinamool Congress has described the rebel MPs as "gaddar" (traitors)

Article Title: Space for secular thought in Bangladesh has shrunk: Exiled writer Taslima Nasreen ahead of Kolkata return
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Exiled Bangladeshi writer Taslima Nasreen on Thursday said the space for secular thought, religious criticism and intellectual debate in Bangladesh had "shrunk dangerously" as she prepared for her first public appearance in Kolkata in nearly 19 years, describing her return to the city as "coming back to my own country. "Nasreen, who will attend a programme in Kolkata on August 1, said the visit symbolised not only a personal homecoming but also the resilience of free expression in the face of attempts to silence dissent. The event is expected to be attended by West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari and noted author Shirshendu Mukhopadhyay.This will be Nasreen's first public appearance in Kolkata since 2007, when protests over her memoir Dwikhandito forced her to leave the city. The book had been banned by the West Bengal government in 2003 for allegedly hurting the sentiments of the Muslim community.Reflecting on her return, Nasreen said Kolkata had always remained home despite her years in exile."I feel as though I am returning to my own country. Bengal has never been divided in my heart by a border or a barbed-wire fence. The door to the eastern part of Bengal remains closed to me, so for now, this part of Bengal is my home," she said."I am returning with joy, but also with pain. Kolkata was not merely a city where I lived; it was where I had a home, friends, readers and a sense of belonging. Nearly nineteen years were taken from me, and no homecoming can return those lost years. I am not returning as a stranger or a guest. I am returning as someone who has always considered herself part of Bengal," she added.The writer said she had never left Kolkata voluntarily and continued to hope for her return over the years."I never left Kolkata willingly; the then West Bengal government forced me to leave the state. Yet I never stopped hoping that one day I would return. Year after year passed, governments changed, and still the door remained closed."Calling her return a victory for freedom of expression, Nasreen said, "So, to return nearly 19 years later and speak publicly in the heart of Kolkata feels almost unreal. To me, it represents the return of a voice that fundamentalists once tried to silence. My presence on that stage will affirm that threats and fatwas may exile a writer for a time, but they cannot erase her ideas."She thanked the organisers and the West Bengal government for facilitating the visit and providing security."I certainly see my return as an encouraging sign. I am grateful to the organisers who made it possible and to the government for providing security. I deeply appreciate CM Adhikari’s willingness to respect and protect the freedom of a dissenting writer, even when he may not agree with everything she says."Nasreen stressed that freedom of expression should be protected as a fundamental right."A writer’s freedom and safety should not depend on the generosity of a government, the ideology of a political party or the permission of a religious group. They must be protected as fundamental rights," she said.Expressing gratitude to India for offering her refuge, she said, "Although I am not a citizen of India, I am deeply moved by the generosity of a country that has given refuge to a persecuted writer like me. I am sincerely grateful to the present West Bengal government for the support and protection it has extended to me."Speaking about the situation in Bangladesh, Nasreen said technological advances had given writers new platforms but had also enabled organised harassment."Technology has given writers more ways to speak, but it has also given organised groups more ways to threaten, harass and silence them. In Bangladesh, the space for secular thought, religious criticism and honest intellectual debate has shrunk dangerously. Freethinkers have been killed, imprisoned, driven into hiding or forced into exile. Fear has become a form of censorship," the writer pointed out.She said religious fundamentalism had gained greater political influence across South Asia while women continued to face restrictions in the name of religion, culture and tradition."The challenges have undoubtedly become more complex. Religious fundamentalism has acquired new political power and sophisticated methods of propaganda. Women are still controlled in the name of religion, culture, family honour and tradition. At the same time, those who oppose fundamentalism are often falsely accused of opposing an entire community," she said.Despite the challenges, Nasreen said she remained optimistic because younger generations continued to question inherited beliefs and resist inequality."I have not lost hope. More young people, especially women, are questioning inherited beliefs and refusing to accept inequality as destiny. Social progress has never followed a straight line; every advance produces resistance. I am not optimistic because I believe progress is inevitable. I am optimistic because people continue to fight for it. Silence guarantees defeat; resistance keeps change possible," she said.Reflecting on her years in exile, Nasreen said, "Exile has made me stronger, but it has also wounded me in ways that strength cannot erase. It taught me that a home is not merely a building or an address."She also urged young readers and writers to defend intellectual freedom."My message would be: question everything. Question religion, tradition, authority, politics and even the ideas you love most. Do not inherit someone else’s prejudices and call them your convictions," she said.Nasreen expressed hope that her upcoming Kolkata visit would not be a one-time event and that she would be able to return to the city whenever she wished.
Article Summary: Nasreen will attend a programme in Kolkata on August 1. The event is expected to be attended by West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari and noted author Shirshendu Mukhopadhyay. Nasreen said the visit symbolised not only a personal homecoming but also the resilience of free expression in the face of attempts to silence dissent.

Jonathan Kuminga's free agency has turned into a two-team race, and both sides have reportedly landed on the same number. The Cleveland Cavaliers and Los Angeles Lakers are said to have capped their offers for the forward at around $18 million annually, well below the $20 million-plus he initially sought after Atlanta declined his $24.3 million team option.Cleveland has already met with Kuminga's side to work toward a sign-and-trade framework, and with Donovan Mitchell now locked up on a four-year extension and Cleveland working to re-sign James Harden, adding a 23-year-old wing with championship pedigree would address one of the roster's clearest needs. Whether Kuminga is willing to come down to Cleveland's number is now the deciding factor.Cleveland entered this offseason searching for a long-term wing and instead watched its roster thin out further. Dean Wade left for the Philadelphia 76ers, Keon Ellis signed with the Brooklyn Nets, and Larry Nance Jr. returned to the Indiana Pacers for a second stint elsewhere. The Cavaliers answered with depth moves like Thomas Bryant and Mario Hezonja rather than a wing solution, leaving the position still open.Kuminga, meanwhile, played just 16 games for Atlanta after arriving in a deal that sent Kristaps Porzingis to Golden State, averaging 13.7 points, 3.3 rebounds and an assist in the team's series against the New York Knicks.The Hawks declined his option rather than pay $24.3 million, pushing him onto the open market at 23 years old with real upside still ahead of him."The Cavaliers will meet with Jonathan Kuminga about working towards finalizing a potential sign-and-trade agreement soon, per Chris Fedor. Cleveland is a main finalist for Kuminga's services alongside the Lakers. Kuminga continues to seek a deal exceeding $20 million annually," NBA reporter Evan Sidery shared.The framework being discussed would have Cleveland structure a sign-and-trade with Atlanta, since the Hawks are already over the roster limit and need the move to return usable value rather than simply losing Kuminga for nothing. Names like Max Strus and Dennis Schröder have been mentioned as pieces Cleveland could send back to make the math work, though nothing has been confirmed as a finalized package.The appeal for Cleveland goes beyond need. Kuminga was on Golden State's title-winning roster before his move to Atlanta, and head coach Kenny Atkinson was part of that Warriors staff. That shared history is viewed as a real factor in Cleveland's pitch, giving the Cavaliers a relationship angle the Lakers can't match.Kuminga gives Cleveland a young, athletic wing still on the rise, a clear upgrade over the depth pieces the Cavaliers have retained this offseason. Slotting him alongside James Harden, assuming Cleveland re-signs him, would give Kuminga an established playmaker to work off of while he continues developing as a scorer.Financially, locking Kuminga in around the reported $15-18 million range rather than his original $20 million-plus ask would let Cleveland add the piece without blowing past its intended spending level, especially with Mitchell's extension now on the books.Cleveland's existing relationship through Kenny Atkinson and its reported asset advantage in sign-and-trade talks give it a real edge over the Lakers, but the gap between Kuminga's original ask and both teams' $18 million ceiling remains the biggest unresolved variable in this rumor.

NEW DELHI: Two-time Olympic medallist Neeraj Chopra led a clean sweep for India in the men's javelin throw qualification at the Commonwealth Games 2026, with all three Indian throwers advancing to the medal round in Glasgow on Thursday.Joining the former Commonwealth Games champion in the final were Rohit Yadav and Yash Vir Singh, ensuring a full Indian contingent in the title-deciding contest scheduled for Friday.Competing in chilly conditions at Scotstoun Stadium, Chopra adopted a cautious approach as he continued his comeback from a long-term back injury.The 2018 Commonwealth Games gold medallist opened with a modest 76.28m, placing sixth after the opening round. He improved to 79.61m with his second throw to climb to fifth and, with qualification already secured, chose to skip his final attempt.Despite receiving the loudest cheers from the crowd while sporting a beanie in the cold Glasgow weather, Chopra focused on doing just enough to progress rather than chasing a big mark.Difficult conditions played a major role throughout the event. With a steady headwind and temperatures around 18 degrees Celsius, none of the competitors managed to breach the automatic qualifying standard of 84m, meaning the top 12 athletes advanced to the final based on their rankings.Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage, winner of this season's Doha and Rome Diamond League meetings, topped the qualification with a first-round effort of 82.84m.India's other two representatives also safely negotiated the qualification round.Rohit Yadav, who boasts a personal and season best of 87.05m, began with 77.04m before improving to 78.37m in his second attempt. Like Chopra, he skipped his final throw after confirming his place in the medal round, finishing ninth overall.Yash Vir Singh, whose personal best stands at 83.72m, improved steadily through the competition. The 24-year-old opened with 73.89m, followed it up with 74.45m, and then produced 78.36m with his final attempt to finish 10th and seal qualification.Chopra is competing in his first Commonwealth Games since winning gold at Gold Coast 2018, having missed the Birmingham 2022 edition because of injury.The former world champion only returned to competition earlier this season after recovering from a persistent lower-back injury that had sidelined him since September last year. He made his comeback at the Doha Diamond League in June, finishing fourth with a best throw of 85.69m.With all three Indians safely through, the focus now shifts to the final, where Chopra will look to reclaim the Commonwealth Games crown while Rohit and Yash Vir aim to challenge for podium finishes and complete a memorable outing for India.

Article Title: "I blew all my money": How did Antonio Brown go from millionaire to bankrupt? Explaining his downfall, legal cases, and more
Article Text:
The rise and stunning fall of Antonio Brown: From Steelers superstar to Miami courtrooms

How did Antonio Brown blow through $100 million?

The off-field chaos that never seemed to stop

What's happened since, and where things stand now

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Antonio Brown was once one of the most unstoppable receivers the NFL had ever seen, a lock for Canton on pure talent alone. Today, the four-time All-Pro is facing an attempted murder charge, has fathered seven kids with four different women amid a mountain of custody battles, and hasn't played a snap in the league since 2021. From MVP-caliber seasons in Pittsburgh to courtrooms in Miami, here's the full, chaotic story of exactly how Antonio Brown's career and personal life spiraled so completely.Antonio Brown once earned an estimated $100 million between NFL contracts and endorsements, cementing himself as one of the highest-paid receivers in football. Today, he's filed for bankruptcy, been forced to sell his mansion, and is facing an attempted murder charge while awaiting a court hearing.In May 2024, Brown filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in Florida, disclosing just $50,000 in assets against nearly $3 million in debt to eight creditors, including a $1.2 million judgment awarded to a moving-truck driver he was found to have assaulted.The situation only got worse from there. In July 2025, a judge converted his bankruptcy case to a Chapter 7 liquidation, and by December 2025, Brown had reached a settlement requiring him to surrender his roughly $4 million Fort Lauderdale mansion so it could be sold off to pay his creditors.That home hit the market in March 2026. On a podcast appearance, Brown admitted flatly that he'd spent it all, saying he "blew everything. "Brown spent nine seasons with the Pittsburgh Steelers, building a Hall of Fame résumé with nearly 1,000 career receptions, six straight seasons leading the league in catches, and four First-Team All-Pro nods. But things unraveled fast once he left.His 2019 stint with the Raiders imploded before he even played a game, a bizarre grievance over an NFL-mandated helmet, frostbitten feet from an unapproved cryotherapy session, missed practices, and a reported blow-up with GM Mike Mayock that got him released before the season started.He signed with the Patriots days later, but lasted barely a week. A former trainer accused him of multiple instances of sexual assault, including one alleged forcible rape, and New England cut him almost immediately (he settled that lawsuit privately in 2021).He resurfaced with the Buccaneers, even winning a Super Bowl in 2020, before his final unraveling in 2021, stripping off his jersey and pads mid-game against the Jets and walking off the field, which got him released for good.The controversy long predated his exit from football. Back in 2018, Brown was sued after allegedly hurling furniture off a 14th-floor balcony in a rage, nearly hitting a toddler below.In 2020, he was accused of physically attacking a moving truck driver outside his Florida mansion over a $4,000 payment dispute, throwing a rock at the truck and pulling the driver from the cab; he pleaded no contest to burglary and battery and was ordered into anger management and a psychological evaluation.He's also been hit with an arrest warrant for allegedly throwing a shoe at the mother of his children and locking her out of their home, and was arrested again in 2023 over roughly $31,000 in unpaid child support. That same year, he was filmed stripping down to his underwear on a public street after a rap concert.His personal life has been just as messy. Brown has fathered seven children with four different women, and virtually every one of those relationships has ended in a custody fight or public blowup.He's feuded publicly and viciously with baby mama Cydney Moreau, telling her to get lost after she asked for rent help for their son, then posting the private messages online for the internet to pick apart.His longtime on-and-off partner Chelsie Kyriss, the mother of four of his kids, has filed for both paternity recognition and sole custody amid allegations he called her an unfit mother; he once posted an explicit photo of the two of them to his public Snapchat. He also inserted himself into Tom Brady's divorce from Gisele Bündchen, posting about her in a way widely seen as a shot at his former teammate.His attempt to own an Arena Football League team, the Albany Empire, collapsed after the league booted him for failing to meet financial obligations.Reports have pegged his net worth as deep in the negative, despite tens of millions earned during his playing career.Then came 2025's most serious chapter yet: Brown was accused of grabbing a security guard's gun after a celebrity boxing match in Miami and firing two shots at a man he'd been fighting with, grazing the victim's neck.An arrest warrant for attempted second-degree murder was issued while Brown was overseas in Dubai, and U.S. Marshals eventually brought him back to Miami-Dade custody. As of this year, Brown remains under house arrest while his legal team pushes a "Stand Your Ground" defense, with a hearing still pending. What was once a can't-miss Hall of Fame trajectory has instead become one of the most spectacular, chaotic falls from grace in modern sports history.
Article Summary: Antonio Brown once earned an estimated $100 million between NFL contracts and endorsements. Today, he's filed for bankruptcy, been forced to sell his mansion, and is facing an attempted murder charge. Brown has fathered seven children with four different women, and virtually every one of those relationships has ended in a custody fight.

Article Title: 10 climbers, including Nirmal Purja, missing after avalanche on Broad Peak in PoK's Gilgit-Baltistan
Article Text:
Who is Nirmal Purja?



Ten international climbers, including renowned Nepal-born mountaineer Nirmal Purja have gone missing after an avalanche struck Broad Peak, one of the world's highest mountains in Pakistan-occupied Gilgit-Baltistan.According to the Alpine Club of Pakistan, the avalanche hit the expedition around midday on Thursday on the 8,047-metre (26,400-foot) Broad Peak in the Karakoram range, the Associated Press reported.The missing team comprises five Nepalese climbers, Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi from Hunza, Omani climber Nathira, American climber Mallory Geis, a Chinese climber identified only as Wang, and another foreign climber, the club said.The team has remained out of communication since the incident. However, a tracking device carried by Purja has continued to show movement, offering a glimmer of hope as rescuers race against time to reach the team.Speaking to Kantipur on Friday, Purja's business partner and Nepal lawmaker Mingma Gyabu Sherpa said data from the mountaineer's tracking device indicated that his location had changed after the avalanche."Initially, it appeared that he had been swept downhill by the avalanche," Sherpa was quoted as saying by The Kathmandu Post. "But after the point where the tracking had stopped, the location appears to have shifted again."Sherpa cautioned that the tracking data could not confirm Purja's condition but said it suggested some movement after the avalanche. He added that detailed information about the incident reached them only on Thursday evening, several hours after the avalanche struck.Poor weather has so far prevented helicopters from taking off, delaying aerial search-and-rescue operations. Sherpa said authorities were preparing to deploy helicopters on Friday morning if weather conditions improved.The club said it was working closely with government authorities to launch an immediate search-and-rescue operation. Its president, Maj Gen Irfan Arshad, and senior officials are coordinating efforts to mobilise helicopters and other rescue resources as soon as weather and operational conditions permit.Purja, also known as Nims Dai, is a Nepal-born British mountaineer and former Royal Marine. He joined the British Army in 2003 and became a Royal Marine in 2009.He rose to global prominence in 2019 after climbing all 14 of the world's 8,000-metre peaks in just 189 days, setting a record at the time.His achievement was later featured in the Netflix documentary "14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible." The record was surpassed in 2023 by a Norwegian climber and her Nepali Sherpa guide.Purja began his mountaineering career in 2012 after trekking to the Everest Base Camp. Instead of returning home as planned, he decided to climb Mount Everest , marking the start of his career as a high-altitude climber.
Article Summary: Ten international climbers, including renowned Nepal-born mountaineer Nirmal Purja, have gone missing. An avalanche struck Broad Peak, one of the world's highest mountains in Pakistan-occupied Gilgit-Baltistan. Who is Lovepreet Singh?



NEW DELHI: "Little disappointed that I couldn't lift in my final attempt," said Lovepreet Singh after narrowly missing out on the gold medal in the men's +110kg weightlifting event at the Commonwealth Games 2026 in Glasgow. The Punjab lifter settled for silver after finishing just one kilogram behind New Zealand's David Andrew Liti, despite breaking the Commonwealth Games snatch record.Lovepreet lifted a total of 388kg, with 176kg in the snatch and 212kg in the clean and jerk.Liti claimed the gold medal with a total of 389kg (166kg in snatch and 223kg in clean and jerk), while England's Andrew Griffith took bronze with 356kg (165kg in snatch and 191kg in clean and jerk).The 28-year-old improved on his bronze medal from the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham by winning silver this time."I thought I would win gold after snatch but it was up to god. Little disappointed that I couldn't lift in my final attempt in clean and jerk, I have lifted more in training," Lovepreet said after his silver-winning effort.Lovepreet dominated the snatch event from the start. He comfortably lifted 168kg in his opening attempt before clearing 173kg.In his third attempt, he successfully lifted 176kg to set a new Commonwealth Games snatch record, taking a 10kg lead into the clean and jerk.With the crowd cheering "Come on Jatta" and "Come on Singh" at the SEC Armadillo, Lovepreet attempted 217kg in his final clean and jerk lift. The lift would have won him the gold medal and also broken the Games record. He managed to clean the weight but could not complete the jerk.Lovepreet Singh hails from Bal Sikander village in Punjab's Amritsar district. His father works as a tailor, while his grandfather earned a living by selling vegetables.Encouraged by his family to pursue sports, Lovepreet started weightlifting at the age of 13 at the DAV Ground.

Patrick Mahomes Sr., the father of Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes, is asking a judge to let him remove the ankle monitor he has been wearing as part of his probation. According to court documents obtained by TMZ, his lawyer said the device has caused serious skin irritation, leaving his lower leg swollen and discolored. The filing also says Mahomes Sr. tried using a skin cream, but it did not improve the condition. His request comes after he completed extra testing ordered by his probation officer, including a voluntary hair-follicle test and a blood test, both of which he passed.The request is linked to the conditions of Patrick Mahomes Sr.’s probation. The former Major League Baseball pitcher was arrested for driving while intoxicated in February 2024. He later accepted a plea deal after admitting to his third DWI charge. Under that agreement, he received five years of probation, including one year of intensive supervision, and was required to wear an alcohol-monitoring ankle device.According to TMZ, Mahomes Sr.’s attorney told the court the monitor has caused ongoing medical problems. The filing says his lower leg became swollen and discolored, and even after applying a cream, the irritation did not go away. At one point, the monitor was moved to his other ankle, but the same problem happened there as well.The court filing also includes a doctor’s note supporting the request. Mahomes Sr.’s probation officer reportedly confirmed that he personally saw the swelling. Before considering the request, the officer asked Mahomes Sr. to take a voluntary hair-follicle test and a blood test. Court records say he passed both tests.Mahomes Sr.’s legal troubles did not end with his original plea agreement. He later violated the terms of his probation by drinking alcohol. As a result, the court extended his probation by two years. He was also ordered to complete a 16-week treatment program and serve 30 days in jail, with credit for time already served.Away from the courtroom, Mahomes Sr. is known for his long baseball career. The 55-year-old played 11 seasons in Major League Baseball, mostly as a relief pitcher, and finished with a 5.34 ERA. He is also the father of four children.His son, Patrick Mahomes II, followed a different path but shared the same love for baseball while growing up. Before becoming one of the NFL’s biggest stars, he was a standout baseball player in high school in Texas. He is now also a minority owner of the Kansas City Royals. Another family connection to baseball is former Minnesota Twins reliever LaTroy Hawkins, who played with Mahomes Sr. and is Patrick Mahomes II’s godfather.The court has not yet ruled on Mahomes Sr.’s request to remove the ankle monitor.

Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers clashed on court during Wings vs Dream showdown

The WNBA's own account is the reason Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers are facing gambling questions this week. During All-Star Weekend, the two stars made a friendly $400 bet on which of their teams would win Wednesday's Wings-Dream game, and the league's social media team filmed and posted it, quoting Bueckers on the terms of the wager.The post ran straight into the WNBA's own rulebook. Section 5(c) of the CBA prohibits players from wagering money or anything of value on the outcome of league games, and the clip showed cash changing hands on camera. The league pulled the video within hours, but by then it had already been screenshotted and recirculated widely.The backlash centered on a simple problem: the league's own staff had broadcast conduct that its own agreement forbids. Fans didn't need to dig for the CBA language once people started pointing it out, and the quiet deletion only made the clip more visible.That leaves commissioner Cathy Engelbert with an awkward choice. Disciplining two of the league's most marketable young players over content her own team promoted risks looking heavy-handed. Ignoring it risks signaling the rulebook only applies when convenient. Either way, the original misstep sits with the league office, not the players who agreed to a $400 bet on camera.The reaction online was immediate and unsparing. Fox Sports host Clay Travis wrote:@ClayTravis shared: "I can’t even comprehend how dumb you have to be to post this video from the league’s official account. Like sub 70 IQ. And how stupid are the players too?! On video bets with cash being shown?"Others zeroed in on the enforcement gap. One user, @krk73, wrote:"Endorsing? Pardon....They aren't endorsing players betting on games. The players are literally betting on games on camera."Another, @SachaVeldhuis, predicted nothing would come of it:"So thats a fine or suspension. But nothing wil happen, all jokes. How dumb is this league. Players getting threats from sports bettors. Tonedeaf league."Several fans also raised double-standard questions, asking whether Fever players would have faced faster discipline for the same clip.Wednesday's game gave the story a second act. In the first quarter at College Park Center, Bueckers switched onto Reese in the post. Reese drove at the smaller Bueckers, who forced a turnover and drew a foul in the process, then celebrated the stop by clapping directly at Reese. Reese approached her, words were exchanged, and no technical foul was called on either player. Dallas carried a 38-32 lead into halftime.The two are reportedly friendly away from the court, having spent time together during All-Star Weekend just days earlier. Reese has drawn attention for in-game needling before, and Bueckers isn't a stranger to it either. Whether the league addresses the wager before their next meeting remains the open question hanging over both teams.

Article Title: Lamine Yamal's net worth at 19 reveals how far he has come from a childhood of struggle and poverty
Article Text:
Lamine Yamal's struggle and net worth (Getty Images)

What is Lamine Yamal's net worth right now?

How much does Lamine Yamal earn from sponsorships and brand deals?

Where did Lamine Yamal grow up and how did his family get to Spain?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Lamine Yamal is 19, a World Cup winner, and sitting on an estimated net worth of something many can only dream of in their lifetime. That figure is only going to grow. In May 2025, Barcelona handed him a six-year contract worth $18 million annually before tax, a deal that landed him tenth on Forbes' list of football's highest earners. The same boy who once slept in an apartment where the bedroom and kitchen shared the same four walls is now one of the most commercially valuable teenagers the sport has ever produced.Celebrity Net Worth puts Lamine Yamal's current wealth at around $15 million, though that number already feels dated. His previous Barcelona contract paid him roughly $1.82 million per year. The club scrapped it. The new deal, signed in the summer of 2025, pays $18 million annually before tax, and that base figure rises further depending on performance bonuses and trophies collected along the way.Barcelona knew exactly what they were protecting. Yamal became the youngest player in the club's history to feature for the first team, doing so at 15 years, nine months, and 16 days. He is the youngest scorer ever for the Spanish national team, the youngest goalscorer in European Championship history, and at 17, the youngest player ever nominated for the Ballon d'Or. Those records are not decorative. They explain why Barcelona moved so fast to lock him down on a long-term deal.His salary is the headline, but the sponsorship income is where the real scale of Lamine Yamal's commercial reach becomes clear. His deal with Adidas is worth approximately $34 million over ten years, making it the anchor of a portfolio that also includes Beats by Dre, OPPO, Powerade, Konami, and UNICEF. For a teenager who has not yet hit his physical peak, that level of brand interest says something about how the market views his trajectory.Most players spend years building that kind of commercial profile. Yamal had it before he turned 18. Brands are not betting on who he is right now. They are betting on who he is going to be for the next decade, and so far, nothing in his career has given them a reason to doubt that investment.Lamine Yamal was born on July 13, 2007, in the Rocafonda neighbourhood of Mataró. His father, Mounir Nasraoui, worked as a building painter of Moroccan origin. His mother, Sheila Ebana, was a waitress from Equatorial Guinea. They separated when Lamine was three. The family lived modestly, in a small apartment where, as Yamal has since admitted, the kitchen and bedroom occupied the same space.The person who shaped him most was his grandmother, Fatima. She arrived in Spain from Morocco with nothing and built everything from scratch. Yamal spoke about it plainly during an appearance on the podcast Resonancia de Corazón con José Ramón de la Morena: "The first to arrive in Spain was my grandmother, who sneaked onto a bus coming from Morocco and managed to reach Mataró."He continued: "She started working 3 jobs so that my father could come, because he stayed in Morocco. And when my grandmother had saved some money, she paid a woman to bring my father and his sister, who came to Spain when they were three years old."That story of sacrifice, grinding and unglamorous, is what sits beneath all the contracts and endorsement deals. Yamal has been open about the fact that providing a more stable life for his family is the part of his success that means the most to him. The money matters. But it matters because of where it came from.
Article Summary: Lamine Yamal is one of the most commercially valuable teenagers in football. The 19-year-old has signed a six-year contract with Barcelona worth $18 million per year. His sponsorship deal with Adidas is worth approximately $34 million over ten years. His family came to Spain from Morocco when he was three.

Article Title: 500,000-year-old elephant bone tool found in England reveals advanced early human technology
Article Text:
pc: Study: Elephant-bone tool (NHMUK PV UNREG 4339) from intertidal deposits at the Boxgrove Waterhole Site

How the 500,000-year-old elephant bone tool was made



Microscopic evidence confirms the elephant bone was used as a tool



Why the Boxgrove elephant bone tool is an extraordinary discovery



What the elephant bone tool reveals about early human intelligence



Half a million years ago, people living in what is now southern England were doing far more than shaping stone into cutting tools. A newly analysed elephant bone from the famous Boxgrove archaeological site suggests they were carefully choosing, modifying and carrying specialised implements made from animal remains to improve their stone-working techniques. The discovery offers one of the clearest glimpses yet of how sophisticated Acheulean technology had become during the Middle Pleistocene. Rather than using whatever materials happened to be nearby, these hominins appear to have selected an unusually durable elephant bone, shaped it into a practical hammer and repeatedly used it to maintain finely crafted flint handaxes. According to the study published in Science Advances, titled “ The earliest elephant-bone tool from Europe: An unexpected raw material for precision knapping of Acheulean handaxes ”, this represents the earliest confirmed elephant-bone knapping hammer discovered in Europe and provides fresh evidence of long-term planning in early human technology. The find also highlights the growing cognitive and technological abilities of early humans, indicating they understood the distinct properties of different raw materials and deliberately matched them to specific tasks. Such choices reflect a level of foresight, skill and innovation rarely documented from this period of human prehistory.The object itself is a fragment of elephant cortical bone measuring just over 10 centimetres long.At first glance it might seem unremarkable, but microscopic examination revealed a sequence of deliberate modifications that separated it from ordinary animal remains.The bone was first broken while it was still fresh before large flakes were intentionally removed from its edges to create a workable shape. The pattern of fractures did not resemble damage caused by trampling, weathering or attempts to extract marrow. Instead, the scars indicated deliberate shaping that prepared the fragment for use as a handheld implement.The researchers also identified fine cut marks that appear to have been made before the bone became a tool. These marks may have resulted from removing remaining soft tissue so the fragment could be prepared for later use, although the authors note that their exact purpose cannot be confirmed.The strongest evidence came from microscopic damage spread across three areas of the bone's surface. The battered patches contained clusters of pits, grooves and fine scratches unlike those expected from natural wear.Using scanning electron microscopy and chemical analysis, the team detected numerous tiny fragments of embedded flint inside these impact marks. As per the study, the combination of pits, parallel scores and flint chips is characteristic of a bone retoucher, a soft hammer used to reshape and sharpen stone tools with greater precision than a hard stone hammer could provide.The pattern of damage also suggested repeated use. The bone was probably employed to deliver relatively light blows during the final stages of maintaining cutting edges rather than during the heavy shaping of new handaxes. The researchers estimate it may have delivered well over one hundred strikes across multiple episodes of tool maintenance before being discarded or left behind.Boxgrove in West Sussex has long been recognised as one of Europe's richest Lower Palaeolithic sites, preserving evidence from roughly 480,000 years ago. Excavations have uncovered hundreds of carefully made handaxes, butchered animal remains, rare human fossils and numerous bone and antler implements associated with flint working.According to the paper, the elephant bone hammer fits into a much broader technological toolkit. Early humans at Boxgrove were already using different kinds of hammers for different stages of tool production. Hard stone hammers helped rough out handaxes, while softer antler and bone tools allowed finer thinning, sharpening and reshaping. The elephant bone appears to have been selected for these more delicate finishing tasks because of its thick, durable outer layer.The researchers also point out that elephant bones are exceptionally rare at Boxgrove, making the choice of raw material especially significant. The bone was probably collected elsewhere, shaped before arriving at the site and transported for repeated use, suggesting that valuable tools were curated rather than simply made and discarded where they were found.The find adds another piece to a growing picture of Middle Pleistocene hominins as flexible and thoughtful toolmakers rather than simple stone knappers. Producing the refined Boxgrove handaxes required careful selection of raw materials, the use of different hammer types for different stages of manufacture and the ability to plan. They argue that the elephant-bone tool demonstrates deliberate resource selection, repeated maintenance of equipment and an adaptable technological approach suited to changing environments. Such behaviour, the researchers suggest, helped these populations expand into cooler parts of Europe and cope with increasingly varied landscapes.
Article Summary: Microscopic evidence confirms the elephant bone was used as a tool. Discovery offers one of the clearest glimpses yet of how sophisticated Acheulean technology had become during the Middle Pleistocene. Early humans at Boxgrove were already using different kinds of hammers for different stages of tool production.

Article Title: Scientists discover ancient silk production in Uzbekistan nearly 2,000 years before the Silk Road
Article Text:
image AI generated

Ancient silkworm cocoons found at Bronze Age Sapalli Tepe in Uzbekistan



Ancient mulberry trees and silkworm cocoons provide evidence of early silk production



Sapalli Tepe discovery suggests sericulture began long before the Silk Road



How domesticated silkworms may have reached Central Asia before the Silk Road



For generations, the history of silk has been told in a fairly straightforward way. Domesticated silkworms emerged in ancient China, silk travelled westward once the Silk Road developed, and the knowledge required to raise silkworms followed the same route. That sequence has shaped both archaeological research and popular history for decades. The story may be far older and rather less linear. Evidence recovered from Bronze Age settlements in present-day Uzbekistan suggests that people in southern Central Asia were already cultivating mulberry trees and raising domesticated silkworms around 2000 BCE. If the findings withstand further scrutiny, they would shift the accepted timeline for organised sericulture in the region by almost two millenniaThe research centres on Sapalli Tepe, a Bronze Age settlement in southern Uzbekistan belonging to the Oxus or Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex. During excavations, archaeologists recovered three ancient silkworm cocoons alongside plant remains preserved in archaeological deposits.According to the new study published in Science Advances, titled “ Silkworm cultivation predating the Silk Road in southern Central Asia (2000 BCE) ”, the cocoons were directly dated to between 1940 and 1765 BCE. Laboratory analyses, including protein fingerprinting, identified them as belonging to Bombyx mori, the domesticated mulberry silkworm, rather than unrelated silk-producing insects.The authors note that the cocoons resemble wild silkworms in appearance, yet their protein signatures align with domesticated Bombyx mori. That combination raises the possibility that these insects represent an early stage in the history of domesticated silkworm populations rather than modern forms.The cocoons were not the only evidence pointing towards organised silk production. More than 1,200 fragments of ancient wood charcoal were analysed from three Bronze Age sites. Among them were charcoal remains identified as Morus (mulberry), the essential food source for domesticated silkworms. The study states that these are the earliest known archaeological remains of mulberry trees from Central Asia.The team also found that mulberry charcoal appeared at all three settlements and became increasingly common through time. Other cultivated plants, including grapes, figs, citrus, barley, wheat, millets and flax, were also identified, suggesting these communities managed a diverse agricultural landscape rather than relying on a limited range of crops.As per the study, the combination of domesticated silkworm cocoons and mulberry remains provides strong evidence that silkworm rearing was taking place locally instead of silk simply arriving through exchange.Traditional historical accounts place the spread of Chinese sericulture into Central Asia during or after the Han Dynasty, when Silk Road trade expanded from the late second century BCE.The new findings challenge that chronology. The discoveries at Sapalli Tepe indicate that communities in southern Central Asia were already practising mulberry-based sericulture roughly 2,000 years before the commonly accepted beginning of Silk Road exchanges.This evidence places silk production alongside other examples of prehistoric movement across Eurasia, including crops, livestock and horticultural knowledge that travelled between East, Central and South Asia during the third and second millennia BCE.The researchers also refer to a previously excavated silk-like textile fragment from Sapalli Tepe, together with numerous textile-making tools recovered from Bronze Age settlements in the region. While these objects alone cannot prove local silk manufacture, they fit the wider archaeological picture emerging from the new analyses.The archaeological evidence currently represents a single well-documented case outside eastern China, making it difficult to identify the exact route by which domesticated silkworms and mulberry cultivation reached Central Asia.One possibility proposed in the paper is movement along the southern slopes of the Himalayas, supported by comparisons with archaeological evidence for mulberry remains and long-standing cultural connections between the Oxus civilisation and the Indus region. At the same time, the researchers emphasise that a northern route cannot yet be ruled out and that additional discoveries will be needed before any dispersal pathway can be confirmed.Reportedly, the evidence from Sapalli Tepe establishes the earliest documented occurrence of mulberry-Bombyx sericulture outside ancient China. Rather than presenting silk production as an innovation that spread only after the Silk Road emerged.
Article Summary: Ancient mulberry trees and silkworm cocoons provide evidence of early silk production. Discovery at Sapalli Tepe suggests sericulture began long before the Silk Road. If the findings withstand further scrutiny, they would shift the accepted timeline for organised sericulture in the region by almost two millennia.

Sorry, I’m being a bit toxic right now, but let's just hope the MrBeast team doesn't see this! Guys, thank you all so much. Instead of conflict, the exchange highlights shared influence and mutual awareness. Clavicular and trans women share a surprising realization about online trends

Article Title: Blindfolds on, stress off: Mumbaikars experience unique art and sound healing
Article Text:
Mumbaikars experienced a unique creative session combining blindfold painting and sound healing. Participants found the workshop offered a relaxing pause from daily stimuli and pressure. Art facilitator Lavanya Rastogi and sound healer Shikha Jhunjhunwala led the therapeutic event. Attendees expressed liberation and a new way of experiencing artistic creation. The event encouraged letting go of perfection and trusting the creative process.

Happy Hikkups

Redbox Cafe, Juhu





For a few hours on Sunday afternoon, a group of Mumbaikars, stepped away from the noise of everyday life and immersed themselves in an unusual creative experience. The Bombay Times Life Styled Club hosted the Feel and Paint Workshop, that combined blindfold painting with sound healing, encouraging participants to let go of perfection, quiet their minds and express themselves freely.The session was conducted by art facilitator Lavanya Rastogi, founder of an art-and-therapy platform, along with yoga therapist and sound healer Shikha Jhunjhunwala.A PAUSE FROM EVERYDAYExplaining the idea behind the workshop, Lavanya said, "This workshop is about a nervous system reset. When you are constantly seeing and hearing multiple stimuli, your mind becomes cluttered. This workshop gives you a small, relaxing pause where you create something beautiful to take home. When you aren't seeing, you stop looking for perfection. Blindfold painting removes the pressure to perform perfectly and helps you let go. It allows you to process your emotions without feeling overwhelmed.”PAINTING TO HEALING FREQUENCIESThe workshop began with Shikha guiding participants through three breathing techniques to help them settle into the moment. Once blindfolded, they painted freely while she played singing bowls and other sound-healing instruments, filling the room with calming frequencies that complemented the creative process.For many, the experience was both therapeutic and liberating. Investment advisor Leena Pathare from Vile Parle, who had never painted before, said, "This was wonderful. I wanted to try something different from my daily routine. I've never painted before, and today I absolutely loved creating this."Former banker-turned-entrepreneur Bhumika Jain from Santa Cruz, who painted bright flowers and shrubs, found the combination deeply immersive. "I love painting and have attended sound healing sessions before, but this was the perfect blend of both. Once I was blindfolded, I experienced painting in a completely different way- I just let everything be, without trying to control it," she said. Recalling what she visualised during the session, Bhumika added, "It felt as though I was running through meadows filled with flowers, with birds chirping all around me. "CREATING WITHOUT JUDGEMENTReal estate developer Raunak Mehta from Juhu attended the workshop with his wife, Avani Saghvi Mehta. "My wife brought me here, and this is the first time we've done something like this together. I used to paint many years ago, so revisiting it in this way was a completely new experience," he said. Avani added, "I loved the sounds. They were incredibly refreshing. I had attended a sound healing workshop before, but combining it with painting made this experience even more special. "Advocate Sweta Doshi from Vile Parle appreciated the freedom that came with painting without expectations. "Blindfold painting means you don't know what's emerging on the canvas, and later you shape it into something you want. It was wonderful to sit with myself, paint to these calming sounds and leave all my worries at home," she said.Another participant, Geeta Bhatia, admitted meditation had never appealed to her. "I'm usually restless and have a wandering mind, but I absolutely loved today's one-of-a-kind workshop," she said.As participants finally removed their blindfolds to discover vibrant, instinctive artworks on their canvases, they left with more than colourful paintings. They carried home a reminder that slowing down, trusting the process and letting go of perfection can sometimes be the most creative act of all.Event Partner:Venue Partner:
Article Summary: Mumbaikars experienced a unique creative session combining blindfold painting and sound healing. Participants found the workshop offered a relaxing pause from daily stimuli and pressure. Art facilitator Lavanya Rastogi and sound healer Shikha Jhunjhunwala led the therapeutic event.

Article Title: 80-year-old farmer injured in leopard attack, forest dept installs cages
